Invaded
in-vay'ded
v. (entered a territory in force; of the Philistines and Amalekites upon Israel, and of the Moabite bands that came in at the year's turn)
From Latin invadere, to go into, from in and vadere, to go. The Hebrew at 1 Samuel 30:1 is pashat, to strip or spread out — the raiding party spreading over the country; the Authorized Version's margin at 1 Samuel 23:27 renders it “spread themselves upon.”

Biblical Definition

The Hebrew verb pictures a raiding force spreading over open country like a stain, and the Authorized Version uses it of the recurring plague of Israel's history. The most important occurrence is the sacking of Ziklag: “when David and his men were come to Ziklag on the third day, that the Amalekites had invaded the south, and Ziklag, and smitten Ziklag, and burned it with fire” (1 Samuel 30:1). What follows is one of the great hinges of David's life. Everything he had was gone, the wives and children of his men were taken, and “David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him… but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God” (1 Samuel 30:6). That last clause is one of the plainest statements in Scripture of what a believer does when there is no comfort available from any other quarter. Elsewhere the word marks the ordinary insecurity of a small nation: “the bands of the Moabites invaded the land at the coming in of the year” (2 Kings 13:20), raiding being seasonal; and Ahaz's reign is measured by it, with the Philistines taking city after city of the low country (2 Chronicles 28:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines invade as to enter a country as an enemy with a view to conquest or plunder, and figuratively to attack or infringe.

expand to see more

INVADED, pp. Entered by an enemy; attacked; encroached on.

INVADE, v.t. To enter a country, as an army with hostile intentions; to enter as an enemy, with a view to conquest or plunder.

2. To attack; to assail; to assault.

3. To attack; to infringe; to encroach on; to violate; as, the king invaded the rights of the people.

INVASION, n. A hostile entrance into the possessions of another.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 30:1 — "And it came to pass, when David and his men were come to Ziklag on the third day, that the Amalekites had invaded the south, and Ziklag, and smitten Ziklag, and burned it with fire;"

1 Samuel 30:6 — "And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God."

2 Kings 13:20 — "And Elisha died, and they buried him. And the bands of the Moabites invaded the land at the coming in of the year."

2 Chronicles 28:18 — "The Philistines also had invaded the cities of the low country, and of the south of Judah, and had taken Bethshemesh, and Ajalon, and Gederoth, and Shocho with the villages thereof, and Timnah with the villages thereof, Gimzo also and the villages thereof: and they dwelt there."

Modern Corruption

1 Samuel 30:6 is quoted as a slogan for self-motivation, when the verse says David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.

expand to see more

David encouraged himself in the LORD his God is regularly cited as an early instance of positive self-talk — a man rallying his own spirits. The preposition is the whole verse. He did not encourage himself with a recollection of past successes or with confidence in his own resources; he strengthened himself in the LORD, and the next verse shows what that meant practically: he called for Abiathar the priest and the ephod and enquired of the LORD whether to pursue. The strengthening produced immediate submission of the decision to God, not a resolve to act on his own judgment. That is the difference between biblical encouragement and morale.

The circumstances are worth stating plainly, because they are extreme. David's city was burnt, his two wives taken, his six hundred men bereaved of their families, and those same men, his only remaining asset, were discussing stoning him. He had also brought the situation partly on himself by his long sojourn among the Philistines. There is no comfort available anywhere in that scene except in God, which is why the verse has served believers for three thousand years. The chapter ends with everything recovered, nothing lacking, small or great, and David establishing a statute for the division of spoil between those who fought and those who stayed with the stuff.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pashat, to strip, spread out, make a raid — 1 Samuel 30:1, 2 Kings 13:20; gedud, a raiding band — 2 Kings 13:20; chazaq, to strengthen — 1 Samuel 30:6.

expand to see more

Hebrew pashat — to strip off, to spread out in a raid; the verb rendered invaded.

Hebrew gedud — a troop or raiding band; 2 Kings 13:20, of the Moabites.

Hebrew chazaq — to be strong, to strengthen oneself; 1 Samuel 30:6.

Hebrew Amaleq — Amalek, the hereditary enemy from Exodus 17 onward.

Latin invadere, to go in — the source of the English word.

Usage

"“The Amalekites had invaded the south” — and Ziklag was burnt with fire."

"“David encouraged himself in the LORD his God” — the preposition carries the verse."

"“At the coming in of the year” — raiding was seasonal, and expected."
